When Power Ends, Accountability Begins The recent investigations and legal action involving former ministers, senior officials and other politically connected individuals, has once again brought an important question to the centre of Sri Lanka’s national conversation: Is anyone truly above the law? But beyond any individual case, there is a much bigger principle at stake. For decades, political power in Sri Lanka has sometimes appeared to create a world where certain people were treated as though they were beyond ordinary accountability. Political office, wealth, influence, connections and access to powerful networks could create the impression that some individuals would never have to answer difficult questions. But political power is temporary. The law must not be. A former President, former First Lady, minister, Member of Parliament, businessman, senior public servant or an ordinary citizen should ultimately stand on the same side of the law. If there are credible allegations of corruption, abuse of public resources or misuse of authority, those allegations must be investigated independently, fairly and transparently. If wrongdoing is established through due process, the consequences should follow—regardless of the person's name, position or political connections. At the same time, justice must never become revenge. An arrest is not a conviction, and an allegation is not proof. Every person accused of wrongdoing deserves due process, the opportunity to defend themselves and a fair determination by the courts. That principle is just as important when the accused is powerful as when the accused is powerless. Yet, if corruption is ultimately proven, accountability cannot stop halfway. The people of Sri Lanka have carried enormous burdens. Ordinary families have watched their savings lose value, struggled with rising costs, worried about their children's futures and endured years of economic uncertainty. When public resources are allegedly stolen, misused or diverted, the damage is not merely financial. Every rupee lost represents an opportunity lost—a hospital service, a school facility, a job, a road, a scholarship, or some small hope that could have improved someone's life. That is why allegations involving public money must be taken seriously. If anyone has unlawfully taken public funds, abused public office or used political influence for personal benefit, then the law should pursue the evidence wherever it leads. There should be no selective justice—neither protection for the powerful nor persecution of political opponents. What goes around comes around is more than a saying. It is a reminder that power does not last forever. The people who once commanded institutions may one day have to stand before those same institutions and answer questions. The people who once had the ability to influence others may one day depend entirely on the fairness and independence of the system. Money can buy houses, cars and comfort. It can buy influence for a time. But it cannot permanently buy peace of mind. Political connections can delay accountability, but they cannot guarantee escape from it forever. Sri Lanka does not need revenge against yesterday's powerful people. Sri Lanka needs justice, transparency and the restoration of public trust. If wrongdoing is proven, those responsible should be held accountable according to law. If allegations cannot be proven, they should be cleared according to law. That is what a mature democracy requires. No position is permanent. No political dynasty lasts forever. No amount of wealth is worth the destruction of a nation. And no individual—however powerful—should be able to claim a permanent exemption from accountability. In the end, titles disappear, power changes hands, wealth passes from one generation to another—and what remains is the truth of what we did with the power entrusted to us. What goes around comes around. Justice may take time, but accountability must never disappear.
